author: basil

original.text: Et separavit Deus inter lucem et tenebras, id est incommixtam naturam illarum, sibique ex contrarietate disparem fabricavit; quippe quas prolixis a se spatiis et destituit et discrevit, sicut dictum est: Et vocavit Deus lucem diem, et tenebras vocavit noctem.

english.text: And God separated between the light and the darkness — that is, he fashioned their nature unmingled, and unlike itself by contrariety; for he both set them apart from one another by long spaces and distinguished them, as it is said: And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.

notes: The Greek bench's answer, in the Latin Eustathius made of it, and it is entirely physical: the division is a fashioning of the two natures so that they cannot mix, and a placing of them at long distances from each other. What Basil will not do is make the darkness nothing. He has just said, a few columns earlier, that night is the shadowing of the air which the sun's setting produces; here the darkness is a nature with a contrary, and the separating is a work on both. Bede's 'not only by a difference of quality but of place' is this sentence in another language, and Bede did not need to be reading it to arrive there — but Angelomus, who did read something like it, attributes it to Clement.
